rows.question: When does my maternity leave start if my due date is 15 November 2026?
rows.reply:
Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) before the birth covers the last six weeks before the expected day of delivery. During those six weeks your employer may not employ you unless you expressly declare that you are willing to work. You can withdraw that declaration at any time for the future.

The six weeks are counted from the expected delivery date on your doctor's or midwife's certificate. For you, that is 15 November 2026, so the period before the birth covers the six weeks leading up to that date. The sources here do not say how the first day is counted. Confirm the exact start date with your employer, and with your health insurer if you receive maternity benefit. For maternity benefit paid before the birth, the health insurer also relies on a certificate from a doctor or midwife that states the expected delivery date.

If the baby arrives earlier or later than 15 November, the period before the birth becomes shorter or longer to match. After the birth, your employer may not employ you for eight weeks. This rises to twelve weeks for premature births, multiple births, or if a disability is medically confirmed within eight weeks. If the birth is early, the time lost before the birth is added to the period after it.

These rules apply to employees. Self-employed women are not covered by the Maternity Protection Act and have to arrange their own cover.

rows.question: How long after birth can we apply for Elterngeld without losing money?
rows.reply:
Elterngeld (parental allowance) must be applied for in writing. The law does not set a cut-off date for applying. Instead, it limits back payment: Elterngeld is paid retroactively only for the last three months of the child's life before the start of the month of life in which the application is received.

The consequence is that any earlier months of the child's life are not paid. An application received during the child's fourth month of life still reaches back to the first month. An application received later loses the earliest months, one for each month of delay.

For context, Elterngeld can be drawn from the day of birth. Basic Elterngeld can be drawn until the child completes the 14th month of life. Elterngeld Plus can be drawn until the child completes the 32nd month of life, as long as at least one parent draws it in consecutive months from the 15th month of life.

The same three-month limit applies to changes to an application: a change can reach back only three months of life before the month in which the change request is received.

Applications go to your local parental allowance office, which decides each case.

rows.question: How much notice do I have to give my employer for Elternzeit?
rows.reply:
Elternzeit (parental leave (unpaid job-protected leave)) is not applied for. You request it from your employer in text form, a set number of weeks before it starts. The law sets two notice periods, depending on when the leave falls. For leave up to the child's third birthday, you must request it at the latest seven weeks before it begins. For leave between the third birthday and the end of the child's eighth year, the notice is at the latest 13 weeks before it begins.

When you request Elternzeit for the period up to the third birthday, you must also state at the same time which periods within two years you will take. If a mother takes Elternzeit straight after her maternity protection period, that period counts towards the two years.

The official family portal explains that text form means a letter without a signature or an email is enough. It adds that the employer must confirm your Elternzeit in writing, and that you should ask for this confirmation. The law itself says the employer must certify the Elternzeit.

There are two exceptions. If there are urgent reasons, a reasonable shorter notice period is possible in exceptional cases. The portal gives premature birth as an example. If a mother cannot request Elternzeit in time, for a reason she is not responsible for, and the leave is to follow directly after her maternity protection period, she can make the request within one week after that reason ends.

The family portal also says different notice rules apply to children born before 1 July 2015. The legal text provided here does not include that transitional rule, so it is not confirmed here. If your child was born before that date, check the transitional rule in the Elterngeld and Elternzeit act (BEEG) or ask your employer.

rows.question: How long is maternity protection after the birth if the baby comes early?
rows.reply:
Mutterschutz (statutory maternity protection period) after the birth normally lasts eight weeks. During this time your employer may not employ you.

The law gives two separate rules that can matter when a baby comes early.

1. Birth before the expected date. The six weeks before birth are counted from the expected date of delivery. If the baby arrives earlier, that pre-birth period is shorter. The days lost are added to the period after the birth. So the protection after birth lasts eight weeks plus the days by which the birth was early.

2. Premature birth in the medical sense. For a premature birth, the period after birth is extended from eight to twelve weeks. The days lost before the birth are added on top of these twelve weeks as well. The same twelve-week rule applies to multiple births. It also applies when a disability in the child is medically confirmed within eight weeks of the birth, but only if the mother applies for it.

The law itself does not define premature birth in the text provided. The federal family portal gives a birth weight under 2,500 grams as an example of a birth that counts medically as premature.

If you are a member of a statutory health insurance fund, maternity benefit is paid for the protection periods before and after the birth and for the day of birth.

rows.question: Can my employer dismiss me while I am pregnant?
rows.reply:
In general, no. Under federal maternity protection law, an employer may not dismiss a woman during her pregnancy. This Kündigungsschutz (protection against dismissal) also runs until the end of the protection period after the birth, and at least until four months after the birth. It also covers the four months after a miscarriage after the twelfth week of pregnancy.

The protection depends on the employer knowing. It applies if the employer knows about the pregnancy when giving notice, or if you tell the employer within two weeks after receiving the dismissal. Missing those two weeks does no harm if the delay was not your fault and you inform the employer without delay. The official guidance adds that the protection applies even if you did not yet know you were pregnant, as long as you were already pregnant when you received the dismissal.

There are narrow exceptions. In special cases not connected with the pregnancy, a miscarriage or the birth, the highest state authority responsible for occupational safety, or a body it designates, can declare a dismissal permissible. The dismissal must then be in writing and must state the reason. The official guidance gives examples such as insolvency, partial closure of the business, a small business that cannot continue without a qualified replacement, or a particularly serious breach of duty. Without that authority's approval, the dismissal is invalid.

If you are dismissed without that approval, the official guidance says you must bring a claim at the labour court, normally within three weeks of receiving the written dismissal. If you do not bring a claim, the dismissal counts as legally effective. You can file it yourself, through a lawyer, or orally at the court office. The guidance also advises contacting the responsible supervisory authority. If the authority did approve the dismissal, you can challenge that approval separately, but this does not replace the claim at the labour court.

Whether a particular dismissal is valid is decided by the labour court. Whether a dismissal is permitted in the first place is decided by the state supervisory authority for occupational safety.

rows.question: Is there an income limit above which we get no Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes. Under the statute, the claim to Elterngeld (parental allowance) lapses if the entitled person had zu versteuerndes Einkommen (taxable income) of more than 175,000 euros in the last completed tax assessment period before the child's birth. If another person also meets the conditions to claim, the claim lapses if the combined zu versteuerndes Einkommen of both people is more than 175,000 euros (BEEG §1 (8)).

The limit refers to zu versteuerndes Einkommen, not gross income. Gross income is usually considerably higher. Your zu versteuerndes Einkommen is set by the Finanzamt and appears in your tax assessment (Steuerbescheid). The assessment for the year before the birth should be attached to the application if you have it.

If that tax assessment is not yet available when you apply, you can still apply. If your application says the limit will probably not be exceeded, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation if it later turns out the limit was exceeded. If it cannot yet be said whether the limit is exceeded, the amount is decided provisionally (BEEG §8 (2) and (3)).

The 175,000-euro figure is the one the statute states for the current case. The federal family portal describes different, higher limits for earlier births. The statute's transitional rules for earlier births are not among the sources here, so this answer does not say which limit applies to a particular birth date. Your Elterngeldstelle (parental allowance office) decides which rule applies to your child and whether the limit is exceeded in your case.

rows.question: How many months of Elterngeld can we get in total?
rows.reply:
Elterngeld (parental allowance) is paid in monthly amounts for the child's months of life, not for calendar months. BEEG §4 sets these limits on how many months can be paid.

Total for both parents together:
- Parents together have a claim to 12 monthly amounts of the basic form of Elterngeld.
- Two further months, called partner months, are added if one parent's earned income is reduced in two of the child's months of life. That makes 14 months of the basic form together.
- Instead of one month of the basic form, a parent can take two months of Elterngeld Plus, the lower monthly variant.

Limits for each parent:
- One parent can have at most 12 monthly amounts of the basic form. On top of that, a parent can have at most 4 monthly amounts of the partnership bonus under BEEG §4b.
- A parent only has a claim if they receive Elterngeld for at least two months of life.

Time windows:
- The basic form can be received until the child completes its 14th month of life.
- Elterngeld Plus can be received until the child completes its 32nd month of life. From the 15th month on, at least one parent must receive it in consecutive months.

Premature births:
- The joint total of the basic form is higher if the child was born well before the expected due date. At least 6 weeks early gives 13 months, at least 8 weeks gives 14, at least 12 weeks gives 15, and at least 16 weeks gives 16.
- In these cases the limit for each parent and the time windows are extended to match.
- The expected due date is the one shown on the doctor's or midwife's certificate.

The number of months your family actually receives depends on your circumstances and on the months you choose in the application. Only the Elterngeld office handling your application decides your individual case.

rows.question: What is the Partnerschaftsbonus and who qualifies?
rows.reply:
The Partnerschaftsbonus (partnership bonus months) gives each parent extra monthly payments of parental allowance when both parents work part-time at the same time. Each payment is one additional monthly amount of the longer-running, lower-rate form of parental allowance, the form that can be drawn for two months in place of one month of the basic form.

What the law requires:
- Both parents work no less than 24 and no more than 32 hours a week, averaged over the month of the child's life.
- Both parents meet the general conditions for parental allowance that the law sets in §1.
- Each parent can receive at most four Partnerschaftsbonus months, and only if they take it for at least two months.
- Both parents must take it at the same time and in consecutive months of the child's life.

Single parents: one parent can receive these extra monthly amounts alone in certain situations. These are:
- the parent qualifies for the single-parent tax relief and the other parent lives neither with them nor with the child;
- care by the other parent would endanger the child's welfare;
- care by the other parent is impossible, for example because of serious illness or severe disability.

In that case the parent must work 24 to 32 hours a week, averaged over the month, in two to four consecutive months. If one of these situations arises while both parents are already receiving the bonus, one parent can continue it alone.

If it later turns out the conditions were not met in every month applied for, the law still treats the requirement for consecutive months as met. Official guidance adds that a month in which either parent worked outside the 24 to 32 hour range must be paid back for both parents. Months in which the conditions were met can be kept, as long as there are at least two of them.

The same guidance says its explanations cover children born after August 2021, and that partly different rules apply to earlier births.

Whether a particular family qualifies, and for which months, is decided by your parental allowance office.

rows.question: How quickly do we have to register the birth at the Standesamt?
rows.reply:
The law requires the birth to be reported to the Standesamt (civil registry office) for the place where the child was born within one week. The Standesamt in the place of birth handles the registration. Its website lists any further documents it needs.

rows.question: Does my Krankenkasse pay for a midwife?
rows.reply:
Federal health insurance law gives women insured with a Krankenkasse (statutory health insurer) an entitlement to help from a Hebamme (midwife). Midwife care after the birth is covered until twelve weeks after the birth. Care beyond that point needs a doctor's order.

If the mother cannot care for the child after the birth, an insured child has its own entitlement to the midwife care that relates to the child.

If you have private health insurance, the official family portal advises you to check with your insurer in advance which services it covers.

Your Krankenkasse decides on the services in your own case. Ask it directly if you are unsure what it will cover.

rows.question: How do we insure the baby after the birth?
rows.reply:
In statutory health insurance, a child is normally covered through a parent's membership. This is called Familienversicherung (free family cover for dependants). The law says children of members are insured if they live or usually stay in Germany, are not insured in their own right, are not exempt from compulsory insurance, are not mainly self-employed, and have no regular income above a set limit. Children are covered this way until they turn 18. Longer periods apply in some cases, such as further education or a disability.

There is one important exception. A child is not covered through Familienversicherung if three things are all true: the other parent, who is related to the child, is not a member of a statutory health insurance fund; that parent's total income regularly exceeds one twelfth of the annual earnings ceiling each month; and it is regularly higher than the member parent's income.

In practice, you first register the birth at the registry office for the place of birth. The official family portal says this must happen within one week. The registry office issues the birth certificate. You need the birth certificate to register the child with the health insurance fund.

Whether your baby is covered through Familienversicherung is decided by the parent's statutory health insurance fund. If the exception may apply to you, for example because a parent is privately insured, this product does not cover private insurance. In that case, ask the insurance fund or the private insurer directly.

rows.question: When are the first check-ups for the baby?
rows.reply:
The first check-up for children, the U1, happens straight after birth. The children's screening guideline (Kinder-Richtlinie) sets out ten check-ups in the first six years of life, each with a set time window and a wider tolerance window.

The first ones are:

- U1: immediately after birth. It should be done within the first 30 minutes after the baby is born. If no doctor is present at the birth but a midwife is, the midwife should do it.
- U2: 3rd to 10th day of life. Tolerance window: 3rd to 14th day.
- U3: 4th to 5th week of life. Tolerance window: 3rd to 8th week.
- U4: 3rd to 4th month of life. Tolerance window: 2nd to 4½ months.
- U5: 6th to 7th month of life. Tolerance window: 5th to 8th month.
- U6: 10th to 12th month of life. Tolerance window: 9th to 14th month.

The guideline says each check-up can only be used within its time window, taking the tolerance window into account. These windows also apply to babies born prematurely. The doctor takes the premature birth into account when assessing the results.

rows.question: What is Mutterschaftsgeld and when do I apply for it?
rows.reply:
Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) is a payment for the protection periods before and after the birth, and for the day of the birth itself.

Who pays it:
- If you are a member of a statutory health insurer, the insurer pays it under the rules of the Social Code, Book V (MuSchG §19(1), SGB V §24i). For women who are employed when the protection period before the birth begins, it is based on average net daily pay over the last three settled calendar months before that period. It is capped at 13 euros per calendar day (SGB V §24i(2)).
- If your average net daily pay is higher than 13 euros, your employer pays the difference as a top-up while your employment continues (MuSchG §20(1)).
- If you are not a member of a statutory health insurer, the federal government pays Mutterschaftsgeld, at most 210 euros in total. The Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung pays this on application (MuSchG §19(2)).
- The payment is suspended for as long as you receive pay subject to contributions, except one-off payments (SGB V §24i(4)).

When it is paid: the protection periods normally begin 6 weeks before the expected due date and end 8 weeks after the birth (Familienportal). For payment before the birth, the decisive document is a certificate from a doctor or midwife that states the expected day of delivery (SGB V §24i(3)).

When to apply: the excerpts I have do not say when or how to apply to a statutory health insurer, and they give no application deadline. Ask your statutory health insurer how and when to submit your application and the doctor's or midwife's certificate. If you are not statutorily insured, the application goes to the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung. Whether you qualify and how much you receive is decided by your health insurer or the Bundesamt für Soziale Sicherung.

rows.question: We are not married. Is my partner automatically the legal father?
rows.reply:
No. Under German law, a man is the legal father of a child if he is married to the mother at the time of the birth, if he has acknowledged paternity, or if a court has established his paternity. Marriage is the only one of these that applies automatically.

If you are not married to each other at the time of the birth, your partner must make a Vaterschaftsanerkennung (acknowledgement of paternity) to count legally as the father. It is voluntary and needs the mother's consent.

How it works:
- He makes the declaration in person at a responsible office, for example the youth welfare office, a registry office, a local court or a notary. The mother must also give her consent in person. The office records both.
- The Vaterschaftsanerkennung can be made before the child is born.
- It cannot be made subject to a condition or a time limit. If it is, it is not valid.
- It does not take effect while another man's paternity exists. For example, if the mother is married to another man at the birth, that man is the legal father.
- Its legal effects apply only from the point at which it becomes effective.

If the father does not want to acknowledge paternity, or the mother does not consent, the child, the mother or the presumed biological father can ask a court to establish paternity.

Being the legal father does not automatically give him parental custody. For unmarried parents, the mother has custody from the birth. Joint custody additionally needs declarations by both parents that they want joint custody, a court decision, or the parents marrying after the birth. The youth welfare office advises on paternity and custody.

rows.question: How do unmarried parents get joint custody?
rows.reply:
If the parents are not married to each other when the child is born, the mother has parental custody alone. The parents get joint custody in one of three ways: (1) both declare that they want to take on custody together, through a Sorgeerklärung (declaration of joint custody); (2) they marry each other; or (3) the family court transfers joint custody to them.

Before the father can share custody, he must be legally recognised as the father. This happens when he acknowledges the child as his own with the mother's consent, or when a court establishes paternity. Acknowledging paternity does not by itself give him custody. A Sorgeerklärung or a court decision is still needed.

The Sorgeerklärung can be made at the youth welfare office or before a notary, for example. It can also be made before the child is born.

If the parents do not both make a Sorgeerklärung, either parent can apply to the family court. The court transfers all or part of custody to both parents jointly if this does not go against the child's welfare. If the other parent puts forward no reasons against joint custody, and none are otherwise apparent, the law presumes that joint custody does not go against the child's welfare. In that case the family court decides in a simplified procedure, without hearing the youth welfare office and without hearing the parents in person.

Your local youth welfare office gives advice on all questions about parental custody.

rows.question: Will our baby automatically be German if we are both Indian citizens?
rows.reply:
Whether your baby becomes German is decided case by case, so we cannot tell you the outcome for your family. Here is the general rule.

German Staatsangehörigkeit (citizenship) is not acquired just because a child is born in Germany. When neither parent is German, the law sets two conditions. A child of foreign parents born in Germany acquires German Staatsangehörigkeit at birth if one parent:

1. has lawfully had their habitual residence in Germany for five years, and
2. holds an unlimited right of residence (or, for Swiss citizens and their family members, a residence permit under the EU–Switzerland free movement agreement).

Only one parent needs to meet both conditions. If the child acquires German Staatsangehörigkeit this way, it is entered in the birth register where the child's birth is recorded. The office that keeps that register decides on the entry for your child.

If the child does not acquire German Staatsangehörigkeit, a separate rule covers residence. If both parents hold a residence permit, a settlement permit (Niederlassungserlaubnis) or an EU long-term residence permit at the time of birth, the child born in Germany is given a residence permit automatically by the authorities. If one parent holds one of these, the child can be given one. If a parent holds a visa or is allowed to stay visa-free at the time of birth, the child's stay counts as permitted until that visa or visa-free stay ends.

The excerpts we have do not cover Indian citizenship law. They also do not cover how Indian citizenship for your child is handled. For that, ask the Indian consulate responsible for where you live.

rows.question: Does our newborn need a residence permit?
rows.reply:
German law sets out several situations for a child born in Germany. Which one fits your child depends on the parents' status at the birth, and the responsible authority decides the individual case.

If the child is German at birth, the residence-permit rules for foreign children do not come into play. A child becomes German by birth if a parent is German. A child of foreign parents born in Germany also becomes German if one parent has lived lawfully and habitually in Germany for five years and holds an unlimited right of residence. Swiss nationals and their family members holding a residence permit under the EU–Switzerland free movement agreement also count. This acquisition is entered in the birth register.

If the child is not German, the residence law has three rules for a child born in Germany:

- If both parents hold an Aufenthaltserlaubnis (residence permit), a settlement permit or an EU long-term residence permit at the time of the birth, the child is granted an Aufenthaltserlaubnis. The same applies if the parent with sole custody holds one. It is granted without a separate application ('von Amts wegen', on the authority's own initiative).
- If only one parent holds one of these permits, the child can be granted an Aufenthaltserlaubnis on the authority's own initiative. Here the law says 'can', not 'is'.
- If the mother or father holds a visa at the birth, the child's stay counts as permitted until that visa expires. The same applies if the parent is allowed to stay without a visa, until that lawful stay ends.

These excerpts do not name the office that issues the permit. Your local immigration office in Hessen can confirm which office is responsible and what applies to your child.

rows.question: We are getting Mutterschaftsgeld. Does that reduce our Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Under federal law, certain maternity benefits are offset against Elterngeld (parental allowance). BEEG §3(1) lists Mutterschaftsgeld (maternity pay from the health insurer) paid under the social insurance code, and the employer's top-up to Mutterschaftsgeld under MuSchG §20, as income that is deducted from Elterngeld. This applies to the amounts due for the time from the day of the child's birth onwards.

There is one exception. The one-off Mutterschaftsgeld of at most 210 euros, which the Federal Office for Social Security pays to women who are not members of a statutory health insurer (MuSchG §19(2)), is not offset.

If the maternity benefits are due for only part of a month of the child's life, they are offset only against the matching part of that month's Elterngeld (BEEG §3(1)).

The official family portal explains the practical effect for benefits received for the same child. If the maternity benefits are higher than the Elterngeld, only the maternity benefits are paid. If the Elterngeld is higher, the difference is paid as Elterngeld on top. Months in which the mother receives these benefits for the same child count as months of the basic form of Elterngeld, even if the benefits are due for only one day of that month. The portal also says the mother's maternity benefits are offset only against the mother's Elterngeld, not against the father's.

Whether and by how much this changes the Elterngeld in your case is decided by the Elterngeld office responsible for your application.

rows.question: Can I work while receiving Elterngeld?
rows.reply:
Yes, working is not ruled out. The law lets a person receive Elterngeld (parental allowance) if they do no paid work or do not work full time. That is one of four conditions in the statute. The others are living in Germany, living in one household with the child, and caring for and raising the child yourself.

The official family portal explains this as part-time work of no more than 32 hours a week. The portal says this explanation covers children born after August 2021. For children born before 1 September 2021, it says partly different rules apply and refers parents to their Elterngeld office.

Working changes how Elterngeld is paid. The full monthly amount, up to 1,800 euros, is paid for months in which the person has no income from work. In months with income from work that is lower than income before the birth, Elterngeld is paid as a percentage of the difference between the two incomes. For this, income before the birth counts up to at most 2,770 euros.

If you state in your application that you expect income from work, the amount is decided provisionally at first. After the payment period ends, you must prove your actual income from work for that time. If you state that you expect no income from work, Elterngeld is paid subject to revocation in case you do have such income.

Whether you meet the conditions, and how much you receive, is decided only by your Elterngeld office.

rows.question: Where and how do we apply for Kindergeld?
rows.reply:
Where to apply: Kindergeld (child benefit) is applied for at the family benefits office responsible for the district where the entitled person lives. If that person has no residence in Germany, it is the office for the district where they usually stay. If neither applies, it is the office for the district where they work. That same office also decides on the claim. In practice, this is the family benefits office of your local Federal Employment Agency.

How to apply: the law says Kindergeld must be applied for in writing. The official guidance says you can apply electronically or on paper, using the family benefits offices' form. You can fill in the form online, then print and sign it. For a newborn child, you can submit the application fully online with a valid ELSTER certificate, without printing or signing by hand.

What to include: the application must give your tax identification number and your child's tax identification number. For a child under 18, these are usually all you need to provide. If your child was born abroad or lives abroad, include a copy of the foreign birth certificate or another official document that certifies the birth. You can send documents online to the responsible office. If the office asks for more documents, it sets a deadline. Missing that deadline can delay your application or lead to it being refused.

Who applies: Kindergeld is paid to only one person per child. If the child lives in the parents' shared household, the parents decide between themselves who receives it.

Applying later: according to the guidance, Kindergeld is paid retroactively for at most 6 months. Earlier months are not paid. To claim back payments, state in the application that you are applying retroactively and from when.

Questions about applying: the Federal Employment Agency has a free service line, 0800 4 555530.

rows.question: What are the Elterngeld rules for a self-employed parent in Bavaria?
rows.reply: We cover federal law, Hessen procedures and the Indian consular track. Bavarian state procedures are not covered, so we cannot tell you how applications are handled in Bavaria. Ask the Elterngeldstelle responsible for your address in Bavaria about local forms and procedures. Elterngeld (parental allowance) itself is federal law, so the federal rules below apply in Bavaria too. Who qualifies: a person who lives or usually stays in Germany, lives in one household with the child, cares for and raises the child, and works not at all or not full-time (BEEG §1). Self-employed income counts: the income used is the after-tax and after-social-contribution total of positive income, including income from a trade or business and from self-employed work (BEEG §2). How much: Elterngeld is 67 percent of income from work before the birth, up to a maximum of 1,800 euros a month for full months with no income from work. The percentage rises for pre-birth income below 1,000 euros and falls, down to 65 percent, for income above 1,200 euros. The minimum is 300 euros a month (BEEG §2). Missing tax assessment: if your tax assessment for the last completed tax period before the birth is not yet available when you apply, the amount is decided provisionally based on the information you make credible. It is also decided provisionally if you expect to have income from work while receiving Elterngeld. If you gave expected income in the application, you must prove your actual income after the payment period ends (BEEG §8). Payments made on the basis that the limits in §1 Absatz 8 will not be exceeded, or that you will have no income from work, can be revoked if that turns out to be wrong (BEEG §8). How long: Elterngeld comes as a basic allowance or a Plus variant. Parents together have 12 monthly amounts of the basic allowance. They get 2 more if one parent's income from work is reduced for two months. One month of the basic allowance can be taken as two months of the Plus variant. Each parent must take at least two months (BEEG §4). Whether you qualify and how much you would receive is decided only by the Elterngeldstelle. We cannot assess your individual case.

rows.question: Can you fill in our Elterngeld application form for us?
rows.reply:
We cannot fill in your Elterngeld (parental allowance) application for you. Completing it means making choices and statements about your family's own situation, and only the responsible authority decides your individual case. Here is what the law says the application must contain.

The application must be made in writing. It must state for which months of the child's life you are claiming the basic variant of Elterngeld, the Plus variant, or the partnership bonus. (BEEG §7)

The parent who applies must sign it. The other entitled parent must also sign to confirm they have seen it, except where only one parent has custody or in the case covered by BEEG §4c. The other parent can apply at the same time, or tell the authority how many monthly amounts they are claiming. If the authority has neither from the other parent, all monthly amounts are paid to the parent who applied. The other parent can then only receive what is left of the total entitlement. (BEEG §7)

The choices made in the application can be changed until the end of the payment period. (BEEG §7)

Official guidance lists the documents usually attached: the child's birth certificate and proof of your previous income, such as pay slips for the last 12 months or, if self-employed, usually your last tax assessment. Further documents may be needed depending on the case. (Familienportal)

The authority that receives the application and decides is the one your state designates, in the district where the child lives when you first apply. (BEEG §12) Official guidance calls it your Elterngeld office. That office also gives advice on parental leave, so it is the place to ask questions about the form itself. (BEEG §12)

rows.question: Based on our situation, will our Elterngeld application be approved?
rows.reply:
We cannot say whether your application will be approved. Only the Elterngeld office that handles your application decides that. What we can give you is the general rule.

Who can get Elterngeld (parental allowance): the law gives four conditions. A person must:
- have a residence or habitual stay in Germany,
- live in one household with the child,
- care for and raise the child themselves, and
- not work, or not work full-time.

The law also sets out exceptions to some of these conditions, for example for people posted abroad and for adoptive parents.

How to apply: Elterngeld must be applied for in writing. Payment is made retroactively only for the last three months of the child's life before the month in which the application is received. Earlier months are not paid.

If you receive a decision and think it is wrong, the official guidance says you can only have it reviewed by lodging a written objection with your Elterngeld office. This must be done within one month of receiving the decision.

rows.question: How much tax will we save if I switch to Steuerklasse 3 before the birth?
rows.reply:
We cannot tell you how much tax you would save by changing tax class. Calculating tax owed or saved, and advising on which tax class to choose, is for a tax adviser or your local tax office, not this service.

What the sources do say is how a tax class change before the birth is treated when parental allowance is calculated. The law says the income tax deduction used in that calculation takes account of the parent's tax class and, where one applies, the factor under the income tax law. Tax class VI is not taken into account (BEEG §2e(3)).

The official family portal explains that if you changed tax class before the birth, the newest tax class is normally used. The older one is used only if it applied for longer than the newer one within the whole assessment period. A further change of tax class after the birth has no effect on parental allowance.

Whether and how this affects your own payment is decided by the parental allowance office that handles your application. For the tax side, ask a tax adviser or the tax office.
